clips.text: A thousand years ago, the star Vael hung whole in the night — and the world of Aethyr slept beneath its light.
Then it shattered. Five burning Shards fell upon the world, and where each one struck, a Dominion woke.
Where the emerald Shard fell, the forests of Sylvaris remembered how to move — and chose their wardens.
Where the crimson Shard fell, the forges of Ashmar burned a thousand years without fuel.
The cyan Shard sank beneath Meridine, into an archive of truths the tide would rather keep drowned.
The golden Shard crowned the Concord of Dawn in borrowed, blinding light.
And the violet Shard fell into the Hollow — where something patient has been waiting ever since.
Now the Shards stir again. The seals are failing. A war with no honest side begins once more.
A thousand years ago the star Vael shattered and its five Shards fell upon Aethyr. The emerald Shard came down in Sylvaris, and the forest grew over it the way skin grows over a splinter.
Tonight the leaves are wrong. A wind out of the southern marshes carries rot, and the great stag Thornmaw has stopped grazing.
You feel it. Say what you feel.
Something crossed the border, and the border let it.
Yes. Come. I will not send you out blind, and I will not send you out alone.
Two of mine are already standing. Send them forward. That is the whole of attacking.
A scout.
Scouts are sent. Remember that word.
By morning the clearing where the blight fell is bare. Not burned, not poisoned — simply refusing.
The Grove heals everything. It has healed worse than this in a single night.
Then why not this?
Because this is not a wound. It is a mark.
Lay a Wellspring every turn. Every turn, without exception. A Caller who forgets is a Caller who watches.
They were not feeding. They stood on the bare ground facing outward, as if guarding it.
A sylvaris sproutling, barely a season old, follows you to the root-line and will not be shooed away.
Warden. What is under the Oak?
The Shard is under the Oak.
I know what the Shard smells like. That is not what is under the Oak.
Thornmaw does not answer. He turns, and the conversation is over.
Thick bark in front. A creature with high Guard survives what it blocks, and the Grove cannot spare what it does not have to.
A man staggers out of the southern treeline with a marsh still drying on him, and the ember-brand of Ashmar burnt into his pauldron. Kaelis Emberborn. Everyone knows that name.
Nyxhollow is not raiding, Caller. They are surveying. There is a difference, and the difference should frighten you.
Ashmar is a month west. Why come here?
Because they are surveying there too, and our fire is going out.
Surveying for what?
For depth.
Thornmaw has not moved since Kaelis appeared. He is watching him the way you watch a fire indoors.
They followed me. I am sorry. They always follow me now.
The next thing across the border does not skitter. It walks upright, it carries steel, and it stops when it sees you — which nothing mindless has ever done.
That is a surveyor's escort.
It is looking at the Oak.
They are all looking at the Oak. That is the entire problem.
It carried no loot and no rations. Only a measuring cord, knotted at intervals, already half used.
At dusk something walks openly up the deer-path with both hands empty, which is its own kind of threat.
Lady Duskveil offers terms. Stand aside from the Oak and Sylvaris keeps every leaf it has. She does not want your forest.
And if we refuse?
Then she comes anyway, and the forest is simply in the way.
Kill it.
It is the first order Thornmaw has ever given you. He does not give orders. He asks.
She said you would do this. She said to tell you she is sorry.
It offered terms and you had it killed before it finished. Why?
Because I have heard those terms before.
When?
Thornmaw walks away.
Watch him, Caller. That was not a warden protecting a secret. That was something frightened protecting itself.
Among the swarm's nest you find oilcloth, and on the oilcloth a map. Not of the forest — of the roots beneath it. Every taproot, every hollow, drawn true.
No outsider surveyed this. This was drawn from underneath.
Then someone here drew it.
Or something here did.
Warriors come up the deer-path in formation, and you recognise their colours before you recognise that they are attacking.
Those are yours.
Those were mine. I have not commanded anything for eleven days.
I did not come north to warn you, Caller. I came north because something walked me here.
They do not rout. They stop, all at once, like a hand letting go.
Kaelis rolls back his sleeve without being asked. The dark is past his elbow, and it is not spreading — it is arriving, in pulses, from somewhere else.
Eleven days. Since I stood at the edge of their dig and looked down.
Then you are already theirs.
I am already something's. Theirs would be simpler. When I stop being able to say so — end it. Say you will.
I will.
Those are Ashmar riders. My riders. Duskveil is paying in coin now instead of fear, and my people are taking it, because a cold forge does not feed anyone.
The southern bog has moved four hundred paces in a night. Trees that stood a thousand years are standing in water now, drowning politely, without complaint.
From here you fight alone. Not as punishment — because they are counting my herd, and I would rather the count were wrong.
Gold on the ridgeline. Aurelian knights, banners high, marching into a war nobody invited them to.
Sylvaris has proven it cannot hold its Shard. Aurelia will take it into safekeeping. Stand down and no leaf burns.
Two armies, one hole. Ask yourself how both of them learned about it in the same season.
From the ridge you can see both digs at once. Nyxhollow from the south, Aurelia from the east. Neither is aimed at the Shard.
They are converging on a point beside it.
Yes.
You knew. You have known since the first night.
I have known for a thousand years.
The Shard did not make this forest. It fell on a battlefield that was already old, and the first Caller lies under it — and the first Caller was not of Verdance.
What was she?
Gloom. The Grove was not grown to protect the Shard, Caller. The Grove is a lid.
A thousand years of stories, and every one of them was the same lie told gently.
The wardens you grew up beside are walking south with black in their veins, in step, in silence.
It is not converting them. It is calling them. The difference is that they want to go.
You find his sword planted at the lip of the shaft and Kaelis already ten paces below it, going down without a torch.
It has been pulling me since the marsh. If it wants me down there so badly, let it have me while I still choose the timing.
Kaelis —
You promised me an ending. This is me taking it first.
Something comes back up the shaft. It has Kaelis' voice and it is using it carefully, like a borrowed coat.
He asked you to end it. You said you would. You are very slow.
What are you?
The thing your warden has been standing on. Ask him how tired he is.
Ravenna Duskveil stands at the shaft with her own dead stacked around her like sandbags. She is not digging. She is filling it in.
Nine hundred years my house has held this lid down from the other side while your forest took the credit. Do you know what your warden did the first night I sent word?
He had your herald killed.
He has had eleven of them killed.
Thornmaw comes through the treeline at a run, and he does not go for the diggers. He goes for Ravenna.
There. Now you have seen it.
Warden. Stop.
A thousand years I stood over her grave, Caller, and every single one of them I stood there listening.
Do you understand? I was not guarding it. I was keeping it company.
I will not hand nine hundred years to a Caller who has held the truth for one afternoon. Show me you can carry it.
You want to fight me while that thing is awake?
I want to fight you because it is awake. If you cannot beat me you cannot hold the lid, and I will not die leaving it to you.
Behind her, the shaft exhales.
No terms this time, Caller. Come on.
She goes down on one knee and stays there — breathing, alive, and for the first time in nine hundred years not alone in this.
Good. Now look behind you.
The shaft is sealed. The lid is holding. And Thornmaw is gone — no body, no trail, only tracks going down.
He has gone to keep it company. Ashmar next, Caller — their forges are going cold, and cold forges mean someone is digging there too.
The Grove endures. The tale turns west, to fire.
You smell Ashmar three days before you see it, and what you smell is wrong: not smoke, but wet ash. Rain has been falling on the city of fire and nothing has been drying it.
The Heartforge still burns at the centre of the caldera. It is the size of a cathedral and it is the colour of a dying coal.
A thousand years, Caller. A thousand years it never once needed stoking, and now we feed it all night and by dawn it has given the heat back.
Given it back to what?
That is the question nobody here likes.
They never came near heat before. Now they sleep in it.
Ashmar has begun rationing heat. The line for a warming-stone runs four streets and does not move quickly.
Third day I have stood here. Yesterday they turned the line away at dusk. Two did not walk home.
Who decides who gets a stone?
The Warlord decides. The Warlord decides everything now.
They were not thieves this morning. Ashmar is four days of cold away from not being Ashmar.
Warlord Draxus reads the decree himself, from the forge steps, in a voice built for exactly this.
The outer holds will be emptied and burned. Their fuel comes to the Heartforge. Ashmar survives as a smaller Ashmar or it does not survive.
You are burning your own villages.
I am burning six thousand to keep sixty thousand. Give me a better number, Caller, and I will read that one instead.
Step aside. We take no pleasure in this and we will do it anyway.
A woman waits at the hold gate with her husband's tools on her back and no husband.
He went down the vein with the third survey. Twelve went. Twelve came back. He was not one of the twelve, and one of them was not anyone.
Say that again.
Twelve went down and twelve came up, and one of the twelve who came up had never gone down.
What is left on the stones does not match any of the twelve, and does not match anything else either.
The vein opens in the caldera floor like a wound that has been kept open on purpose. Warm air comes out of it in slow, even pushes.
That is not a draught, Caller.
No. That is breathing.
Word comes up from the coast: Meridine has closed the sea. Tide hulls sit in a ring around Ashmar's harbours, and they are not firing.
A siege without a shot. They mean to watch us go cold and then walk in.
Or they mean nothing to leave. Warlord — they are facing outward.
The Tide envoy comes ashore alone, robed to the fingertips, carrying a coral staff and no weapon.
We are not besieging you. We are containing you. There is a difference, and you will like it less.
Containing what?
Whatever comes up that vein when your fire finally fails. The Archive has a word for it. I am forbidden to say the word.
Your Heartforge has no fuel source. It never had. Meridine measured the mountain nine hundred years ago and the mountain does not produce a tenth of what you burn.
Then where has the heat come from?
Up. From something that has been giving it to you, without complaint, for a thousand years.
Giving?
I chose that word carefully, Caller.
Draxus does not wait for the argument to finish. Emberhold goes up at dusk, and the column of smoke is the brightest thing in Ashmar for the first time in a season.
Four hundred souls, and the Heartforge came up two shades. Say it was not worth it. Say it to the sixty thousand.
It came up two shades for one night.
Then we will need more holds.
By morning the city wears two colours. Draxus holds the forge and the granaries. The holds hold the roads.
A civil war over a fire that is going out either way. There is a joke in that and I cannot find it.
The descent takes a day. The walls are warm, then hot, then warm again — and the warmth arrives in slow, even pushes, the same rhythm as the mouth above.
From here you go alone. My order permits me to observe. It does not permit me to help, and I am sorry for the distinction.
The vein opens into a chamber that is not a chamber. The walls move. They have been moving for a thousand years, slowly, in the rhythm of the heat.
Ashmar has not been mining.
No. Ashmar has been drawing. And it has been letting you.
Understand what you are looking at. The fire is not failing. It is being withheld.
Why would it stop now?
Because a cold city digs. Because a starving Warlord burns his own holds and calls it arithmetic. Everything Ashmar has done this season, it did because the heat stopped.
It wanted us to come down here.
It has wanted that for a thousand years. This season it simply asked.
A man walks out of the deep dark of an Ashmaran vein, a month's travel from the shaft he descended, and he is not out of breath.
Caller.
You went down under the World-Oak.
I did. I have not walked a single step since. It is one place down here. Sylvaris, Ashmar, Meridine — one room with a thousand doors, and we built our cities on the doors.
In the fine grey ash of the chamber floor there are hoofprints. Enormous ones. They come from the direction of Sylvaris and they go deeper.
Thornmaw.
He passed through eleven days ago and he did not stop. He is the only one down here who knows where he is going.
Meridine's order is to flood the vein. Sea water, all of it, until Ashmar is a lake and the door is shut.
Sixty thousand people live on top of that door.
Yes. I have been carrying that order in my sleeve for nine days and I have not read it aloud once.
Then don't.
Give me the alternative and I will burn it in front of you.
Let the Heartforge go out.
Ashmar freezes.
Ashmar freezes for one winter. The draw stops, the wound closes, and it has nothing left to bargain with.
It will not simply allow that, Caller. It has spent a thousand years making sure we could not survive without it.
Draxus has the Heartforge stoked to a height it has not reached in living memory. Every hold in Ashmar is burning to feed it.
You want me to let it go dark. I will do the opposite. I will burn so hot the thing below gives back everything it has taken.
You will wake it.
Then it will be awake, and cold, and in my city — where I have sixty thousand and a mountain of fuel.
Kaelis steps between you and the forge stair, and the black in his veins has reached his throat.
It is using me to hold this door. I can feel exactly how it intends to do it.
I promised you an ending.
You did. But not yet — I have one thing left that it does not expect. Take the stair. I will hold the door shut from this side.
Draxus waits at the top of the forge stair with the Heartforge roaring white behind him, and he looks, for the first time, like a man who has done the arithmetic twice.
I know what it is. I have known since the third survey. Do you imagine that changes what a Warlord is for?
Let it go out, Draxus.
And be the man who froze Ashmar. No, Caller. Take the forge from me if you want it dark.
Sixty thousand, Caller. Be sure.
The Heartforge goes out at the ninth hour of the night. A thousand years of light, and the sound it makes going is almost nothing at all.
Cold. So this is what the rest of the world has been doing all along.
Deep below, the drawing stops. The wound begins to close. And somewhere further down, something that has been patient for a thousand years turns its attention elsewhere.
It will look for another door. There are three left, and mine is the one made of paper.
Ashmar endures, and shivers. The tale turns to the deep water.
Meridine floats above its own library. Beneath the hulls, shelves go down further than light does, and every tablet on them glows faintly, because a thing written in Meridine is a thing kept.
Nine hundred thousand records, Caller. I could tell you the count to the last one.
Could you yesterday?
That is precisely the problem.
A tablet in the third vault has gone half blank. Not smashed, not stolen — the ink is simply thinning, letter by letter, while you watch it.
What did it say?
I read it four days ago and I cannot tell you. That is not forgetting, Caller. I know exactly what forgetting feels like.
You catch her in the ninth vault with no bag, no cart, and nothing in her hands.
I am not here to take anything. Lady Duskveil sent me to check whether one particular page still exists.
Which page?
If I say it aloud in this room it will be gone by morning. That is how it works here. Surely you know how it works here.
You sit in the reading room with a single tablet and watch it for an hour. Nothing happens. Then you read it aloud, and the line you read fades while your mouth is still shaping it.
Now you have seen it.
It goes when it is read.
It goes when it is *known*. Something is reading through us, Caller, and it does not leave what it has taken.
She takes the Ashmar flood order out of her sleeve, still sealed, and drops it into the black water of the vault.
Sixty thousand. I told you I would burn it in front of you. There is no fire left in Ashmar, so this will have to do.
Your order will ask.
My order will not remember asking.
Aurelian sail comes over the horizon in a line, and it does not slow at the harbour boom. It goes through it.
Meridine has been keeping records it had no right to keep. Aurelia will take the Archive into safekeeping.
That word again.
The Inquisition does not loot. It goes straight down, past nine centuries of trade ledgers, to a vault it should not know about.
They have a shelf number.
They have *our* shelf number. Someone in this Archive gave it to them.
The vault holds one tablet on an empty shelf built for six hundred. It is a contract. It has five marks on it.
Sylvaris. Ashmar. Meridine. Aurelia. Nyxhollow. All five.
Signed nine hundred and eleven years ago, and every copy of it has been erased since — by us.
What did the five of us agree to?
The clause is blank. We erased that too.
You should hear it from me. The erasures are not an attack. They are my office. I am the ninth Keeper of the Erasure and I have unmade eleven thousand records with my own hand.
You have been destroying your own history.
I have been starving something that eats it. A fact nobody has written down is a fact it cannot read.
In the deepest vault the shelves are not empty. They are full — of tablets Meridine never wrote, in Meridine's own hand, recording things nobody alive has done yet.
It has been keeping its own copy.
Nine hundred years of erasure. And it simply wrote them out again behind us, one shelf lower, every single time.
Below the last shelf the floor is silt, and across the silt, unhurried, go the prints of something enormous with hooves. They do not disturb the water.
He was in Ashmar eleven days ago.
He was in Sylvaris a month ago. Caller — it is one room down here, and your warden is walking it faster than we can sail.
The second archive has a map, and the map is the only thing on it that has never been erased, because the thing that drew it wanted it kept.
Every capital is on a door. All five. We did not settle where the Shards fell. We settled where the doors were.
We were placed, Caller. Like weights.
In the second archive, the Ledger of Five is not blank. The clause is there, written out fully, in nine hundred year old ink.
Do not read it aloud.
It is already read. It has always been read. That is the whole point of this shelf.
The clause is short. Nine hundred years of erasure to hide four lines.
"Each city shall sit upon its door. Each city shall give what is asked. Each city shall forget the asking. The fifth shall keep the count."
The fifth. Nyxhollow.
Ravenna Duskveil's house has kept the count for nine hundred years while the other four called them the villains of the story.
Aurelia reaches the second archive an hour behind you and does not pause at the shelves. They begin loading them.
Every word of this returns to Aurelia. A truth this size cannot be left with a city that erases things.
You are about to carry nine hundred years of its own writing into the one capital that has never once erased anything.
One line in the second archive has been struck through by a different hand — an old hand, a frightened one.
The name of the first Caller. The one buried under Sylvaris. Someone tried to take it out of even *this* record.
Who strikes out a name in a library nobody knows exists?
Someone who has been down here a very long time.
Every tablet in the Archive goes blank at once, from the deepest shelf upward, and the blankness keeps rising.
It has finished reading. It does not need the copies any more.
It reads what is known. It cannot read what no longer exists to be known. There is one record left that it has not taken.
The name.
In my head, Caller. Only there. And I am the ninth Keeper of the Erasure, and I do know how to unmake a record.
Numen —
Tell Duskveil the count was kept honestly. Tell her Meridine is sorry it took nine hundred years to say so.
Where Numen was standing there is an absence, and the absence is wearing her robes.
She unmade herself to keep four syllables from me. Do you know how nearly that worked?
It worked.
It cost her everything and bought you a season. Yes. Call that working, if the word helps.
Four cities fed me and forgot. The fifth counted. And one warden sat on a lid for a thousand years and talked to me every night of it, which was kinder than any of you managed.
Thornmaw.
He is ahead of you. He has been ahead of you since the Grove. Ask yourself, Caller — ahead of you, or leading you?
Her name is already gone, you know. You will not get that one back.
The blankness stops rising. Ink returns to eleven shelves and no further, and one of the restored tablets is a duty roster with a name on it that nobody in the room can read.
Meridine will rebuild the Archive. It will take four hundred years and they will start tomorrow.
The Archive endures, thinner. The tale turns to the light.
Aurelia has not known darkness in nine hundred years. The Halo hangs above the high spire and the light it throws does not cast shadows, which visitors find beautiful for about two days.
You come from Meridine carrying bad news, and the Inquisition came back yesterday carrying eleven barges of shelves. Tell me which of you I should be more afraid of.
The barges.
Yes. I was hoping to be wrong.
Aurelia writes everything down and destroys nothing. The Wall of Edicts runs the length of the sanctum and it is nine hundred years deep in gold leaf.
Every law you have ever passed.
Every law, every census, every confession. The first commandment of Aurelia is that a thing recorded cannot be taken from you.
In Meridine they proved the opposite.
At the fourth hour the Halo stutters. For the length of one breath, Aurelia has shadows. Nine hundred years, and nobody alive has seen their own.
Note the hour.
Why the hour?
Because it is the eleventh time this season and I have all ten others written down, and they are getting closer together.
The Inquisition parades the Meridine shelves through the Ivory Gate. Scribes have been copying them onto the Wall since dawn.
Nine hundred years of a drowned city's cowardice, brought into the light. Every erased word restored.
You are feeding it.
I am recording the truth. If your enemy is harmed by truth, Caller, examine which side you are on.
I am going to tell you something that would end me if the Inquisition heard it. I have been destroying records for four hundred years.
Aurelia's first commandment.
I know what it is. I wrote the modern wording of it. And every decade I take eleven or twelve pages off that Wall and I burn them, and I have never once been caught, and I would do it again tonight.
She takes you up the spire to the Halo, and this close it is not a ring of light. It is a mechanism, and it is under strain.
It is not a blessing. It is a lock.
On what?
On the fourth door. Aurelia was built directly on top of it, and the light has been holding it shut since the founding.
The founding miracle. Aurelia teaches that the light was given to us for our virtue. It was not given. It was lent.
Lent by whom?
By the woman buried under Sylvaris. Every ray over this city for nine hundred years has been hers, and we have spent it, and we have never once said her name at a service.
They come for Seraphel at the sixth hour with a charge sheet four hundred years long and every entry on it true.
The Lightkeeper has been burning Aurelia's memory. She will answer for eleven thousand pages.
Twelve thousand, four hundred and six. If you are going to hang me for it, hang me for the correct number.
While Aurelia argues about a charge sheet, the thing under it walks up to the Ivory Gate in daylight and knocks.
The gate has never been closed.
I am aware. Close it.
The gold leaf on the Wall of Edicts begins to lift, letter by letter, and hangs in the air of the sanctum like a swarm.
It is not stealing them. It is *finishing* them. Nine hundred years of Aurelian record, read in one night.
The Chosen are holding the lower city. From here up, the spire is yours alone.
Whatever you meet on these stairs, it will be wearing something you trust. That is what it does with a city that writes everything down — it knows exactly who you would open a door for.
The Inquisitor holds the middle landing with forty knights and the Halo flickering above all of them.
I have read the Meridine shelves. All of them. I know what the light is and I know what we owe.
Then stand aside.
And tell six hundred thousand faithful that their salvation was a loan from a corpse? No, Caller. Some truths are load-bearing and this one is not mine to pull out.
The Inquisitor is dying on the landing and he is still arguing, because he is Aurelian and that is what they do.
The clause. The fifth shall keep the count. Do you know what the count *is*, Caller? It is not a tally of tribute.
Then what?
Years. Duskveil has been counting down.
The pact was signed nine hundred and eleven years ago. The lock was cut for nine hundred.
It expired eleven years ago.
Eleven years ago the Grove's moss stopped growing back in one clearing and nobody thought it was worth a letter.
Thornmaw is standing on the upper stair with his flanks steaming in the cold, and he does not look surprised to see you.
You are four days later than I hoped.
You have been ahead of me since Sylvaris.
I have been *opening* doors ahead of you since Sylvaris. Do not thank me yet. Ask me why.

A thousand years I stood on her grave and listened to her. She is not a monster, Caller. She is a woman who was buried alive to hold something down, and five cities agreed to keep her fed and forget her name.
She has been erasing archives and hollowing people.
She has been *calling*. For nine hundred years. In every language any of us could hear. What would you have sounded like, by the end?
Warden. Finish it. What is under her?
I do not know. She would never say. In a thousand years of nights, that is the only question she refused.
But she said this: if she is ever freed, someone must be in the ground before she leaves it. Someone willing.
The Halo tears. Aurelia has shadows for the first time in nine hundred years and they are all pointing the same way — down.
Four hundred years I burned pages to buy this city time, and it bought eleven. Take the spire, Caller. I will hold what is left of the light.
She walks into the broken Halo and the mechanism takes her the way a lock takes a key — completely, and without ceremony.
Tell Aurelia the truth. All of it. We were never owed the light. Tell them, and then let them decide what kind of city they want to be in the dark.
What is left of the Halo speaks, and it uses Seraphel's voice because it has just finished reading her.
Four cities. Four doors. Your warden opened three of them for you and you called it help.
He opened them so I could close them.
He opened them so you would be standing at the fifth when the count runs out. Go to Nyxhollow, Caller. Everyone else already has.
She gave you an instruction with her last breath. Ask yourself who was listening when she said it.
The Halo goes out. Aurelia stands in its first darkness in nine hundred years, and the shadows are ordinary, and long, and harmless.
Three doors shut. One left, and it is the one that has been counted down to.
You are going to tell me why you opened them.
In Nyxhollow. In front of Duskveil, so that there is a witness who can stop me if the answer is bad enough.
Aurelia endures, in the dark. The tale turns at last to the thankless city.
You have been told about Nyxhollow your whole life. Black spires, a violet moon, a people who traffic in rot.
What you find is a city with clean streets, full granaries, and a watch that changes on the hour, every hour, without fail. It is the most disciplined place you have ever stood in.
Four capitals spent nine hundred years describing this city to each other. None of them ever visited.
The heart of Nyxhollow is not a palace. It is a hall of black glass ledgers, nine hundred years deep, and every page is a tally.
The count.
The count. Meridine erased its history to starve her. Aurelia wrote everything and fed her. We simply counted, every year, without missing one.
Nine hundred entries. What is the unit?
Years remaining.
Then it reached zero —
Eleven years ago. And I have been writing negative numbers in this ledger ever since, alone, while four capitals argued about trade tariffs.
I asked for a witness. Here is the confession. I opened the first three doors. Sylvaris, Ashmar, Meridine — I went ahead of the Caller and I unsealed each one.
I know. I have been watching you do it.
You *knew*?
I have counted every door he opened. It is the only reason the fifth has not torn. They had to open in order, and slowly, or this one takes the whole coast with it.
Ravenna takes you to a wall of names. It is not a memorial to war. Every name is a Duskveil, and there is one per generation, without a gap, for nine hundred years.
Your family has sent one down. Every generation.
Her condition was that somebody willing had to be in the ground. Not a prisoner. Not a sacrifice. Willing. Four cities agreed to that clause in an afternoon and then went home.
The final name on the wall was carved eleven years ago and the stone dust has not been swept from under it.
Who was she?
My sister. She was nineteen. She volunteered because the count had run out and I was needed up here, and because one of us had to and she got to the door first.
The violet Shard hangs in a shaft of still air under the city, and it is not glowing steadily. It pulses, unevenly, like something breathing badly.
Ten years it held that rhythm. This season it began to stutter.
Riders arrive from Sylvaris, Ashmar, Meridine and Aurelia within the same day. Nine hundred years of silence, and now everyone has an opinion.
They want to know what Nyxhollow intends to do about it. Read the first line of every letter. Go on.
They all begin by asking whose fault it is.
Beneath the Heartshard the fifth door is not a shaft or a vein or a vault. It is a plain stone stair going down, well maintained, with a handrail worn smooth by nine hundred years of use.
Somebody has swept these steps.
Somebody sweeps them every week.
Every landing has a lamp. Every lamp has oil. Somebody has been coming down here, alone, every week, for eleven years, to keep the lamps lit for a sister who cannot see them.
Ravenna.
Do not.
Past the last lamp the stair keeps going, and the guard does not.
From here it is one at a time. That is not a rule of mine. It is a rule of the place.
She is nineteen. She has been nineteen for eleven years. She is sitting with her back against the stone with her hands open on her knees, and she is entirely, unbearably awake.
Ravenna. You are late with the oil.
I am four days early.
Oh. Then it is worse than I thought.
Ten. Grandmother did ten. Her father did ten. Nobody has ever done eleven, and there is a reason nobody has ever done eleven.
What happens at eleven?
You stop being able to tell which of the two of you is doing the calling.
Beyond the sister, in the deepest chamber, there is a woman in the stone. She has been there for a thousand years and she turns her head when you come in.
You are the one who has been shutting my doors.
I am.
Good. Now sit down, because you are about to be very angry with four cities and I would rather you were sitting.
Tell me what you are holding down.
Nothing.
Nothing.

There is nothing under me. There never was. I told five kings there was a horror beneath this stone because it was the only thing that would make them build cities on top of the doors instead of digging them out.
A thousand years. You never told me that.
You would have stopped visiting.
Me. Not on purpose. I have been calling for nine hundred years and nobody came, and a voice that is never answered does not stay a voice. It becomes weather.
The blight. The erasure. The forge going cold. All of it was —
A woman in a hole, asking. Yes. I am so sorry about your friend.
Then let me take the stone. I have sat over you for a thousand years already. I am practised.
You are not willing, old friend. You are loving. It is a warmer thing and it is the wrong shape for this lock.
Explain the difference.
Willing means you could leave and you choose the stone anyway. You have never once believed you could leave.
I have kept the count for nineteen years. I have carried oil down four hundred and twelve times. I could walk up that stair tonight and be Queen of Nyxhollow until I died old.
Get up, little sister. You are relieved.
Ravenna —
Eleven years. You did eleven. Nobody has ever done eleven. Go and be nineteen somewhere with weather in it.
Nine hundred years of unanswered calling does not simply disperse because somebody finally answered. It has been a thing in its own right for a long time now.
It is not mine any more, Caller. I made it and it left home. You will have to put it down yourself.
It goes up into the Heartshard and wears it, and nine hundred years of Nyxhollow's patience turns its face toward you.
Five cities heard me and four of them looked away. I am what is left when you do that for long enough.
I know. Someone is holding the stone now.
Then you have fixed the cause and left the consequence standing in front of you. How very like all five of you.
Answer me properly, then.
The Heartshard steadies. Under Nyxhollow a woman who has been nineteen for eleven years stands up, and above her a queen sits down with her hands open on her knees.
Sylvaris, Ashmar, Meridine, Aurelia, Nyxhollow. Five doors shut, and one of them shut honestly. Do not let them forget which.

I will stay. Not for the lock — she is right, I was never the right shape for it. I will stay because somebody should be down here who chose to be, and because I have four hundred and twelve lamps to keep lit.
You climb the well-kept stair alone. Behind you, for the first time in a thousand years, there is conversation in the dark.
The five endure. Set One is closed.
The stair ends in morning. For the first time, nobody below it is alone. Above it, five cities are preparing five different accounts of what happened.
I thought the sky would have changed more.
It has only had eleven years.
Then it has had time to learn something.
At the gate the watch asks for Ravenna's seal. Her sister sets an oil flask on the captain's desk instead.
She is alive. She is staying. Those are different statements. Write both.
They will ask who rules now.
They may begin by asking who needs breakfast.
We are taking people out, not bringing an army in.
Then let them see us put the weapons down afterward.
The watch lowers its spears one at a time. Nobody has taught them an order for this.
Keep the stair open. A duty without an exit becomes something else.
I will put that in the first letter.
Aurelian riders arrive before the ink dries. Their warrant calls the stair a strategic asset. The flask has left a ring over the word asset.
I did not sign that.
Your seal did.
Then my seal has acquired ambitions. Help me disappoint it.
A command can be legal and still require a refusal.
Let this be the first refusal they record accurately.
The warrant is folded rather than burned. Numen will need evidence; the riders will need a way to admit they were wrong.
There must be a table where none of us owns the chairs.
I know four cities that will object.
Before leaving, you place a spare lamp at the stairhead. Below, Thornmaw calls up to ask whether the roof is still there.
Most of it.
Good. We shall need somewhere to meet when she can come upstairs.
You send five invitations. The fifth goes down the stair, with enough oil for a week.
The roofless Hall of Measures has not hosted a council since the roof fell. This recommends it to everyone for different reasons.
No acoustics for a grand speech. No gallery for applause. Excellent.
No roof for rain.
We can repair something while we argue. It may be a useful precedent.
The Concord has posted guards at the public entrance. At the servants' entrance its own masons wait in the rain.
The hall belongs to the city.
And the city belongs to the light.
Then the light can queue with the masons.
Keep the door behind us open.
So they can leave.
The captain withdraws. The masons enter, and the first common work of the five cities is an argument about drainage.
I shall preserve that in full.
You would.
A Pyre escort brings a chair of black iron and demands the place nearest the exit. Kaelis moves it beside the empty fifth chair.
Ravenna is not a vacancy. Her sister carries her words until she can carry them herself.
And Thornmaw?
He asked us to leave room for antlers. I have done what I can.
We did not cool the forge to warm a different throne.
Then give them a place where they can hear that.
The iron chair stays. The escort takes ordinary stools. Nobody loses a seat to make room.
Five voices. No deciding voice.
A difficult system. I am beginning to trust it.
They agree to build a seal renewed by living people. Nothing may be hidden in its wording. Anyone may withdraw.
And if someone withdraws at the wrong moment?
Then we make something strong enough to survive an honest answer.
Numen writes the condition above the signatures, where nobody can mistake it for a footnote.
The treaty is read to an orchard that has spent three seasons feeding soldiers. There is little left to promise it.
Thornmaw sent instructions.
He always sends instructions. Did he send himself?
He is keeping a different promise today.
The rootkeepers will lend strength only if the orchard receives the first water forever. Beside the channel a village sets out empty jars.
Forever is a large word to write beside a thirsty child.
The roots do not know where the boundary is.
Then we must not teach them the wrong one.
Do we have to break the trees?
No. We have to stop the people speaking for them.
The gate lifts. Water reaches the orchard and the jars. The roots drink last and, to the keepers' embarrassment, survive.
Perhaps we asked them the wrong question.
Ask again tomorrow.
Under the oldest tree the old calling has hardened into a knot. It repeats Thornmaw's silence in the voices of everyone he tried to protect.
I cannot be there. I can tell you where to cut.
You are speaking through a root.
I am learning to delegate.
Do not cut the living root beside it. They have grown together.
I can see the difference.
The knot opens around a green shoot. The old tree has been growing toward water, not toward the Shard.
My vow is to tend what can grow without me.
Then you will have to let us make mistakes.
The orchard sends no royal seal. It sends a basket of seeds, with instructions for giving half away.
No penalty if the seedlings die?
Try again. That is the penalty. It is also the work.
The first vow travels to the roofless hall wrapped in damp cloth. It needs checking every morning.
Ashmar's great forge is dark. Inside its firebox the smiths have built a smaller kiln, and are ashamed of how little it lights.
It cooked three hundred dinners yesterday.
It used to make sunspears.
Three hundred people noticed the difference.
Draxus has closed the charcoal road. He calls the fuel a military reserve. The hospital calls it a winter.
You cannot hold a city with soup.
No. You can feed one. I have spent too long confusing the tasks.
We need the road, not his surrender oath.
Leave a way back to the city. These are our smiths.
Then give them something worth returning to.
The first carts go to the hospital. The second go to the kitchens. The army receives the third and discovers it can wait.
Write every delivery down. No heroic exceptions.
That will be a remarkably dull ledger.
Aurelian engineers offer a radiant furnace. Its contract binds Ashmar's gates to the Concord for a hundred years.
I sent engineers. I did not send owners.
They brought both qualifications.
We can keep the design and refuse the terms.
Your knowledge will be credited. Your claim will not.
That is a distinction Ashmar should have learned sooner.
The engineers leave a drawing on the workbench. One stays to learn how a charcoal fire is banked for the night.
My vow is to spend strength where it warms someone other than me.
Tomorrow, too.
At midnight Kaelis returns to the dead forge alone. A pale warmth rests inside her gauntlet. She closes it before anyone arrives.
We remember what your city sounded like when it was warm.
So do I.
She signs the second vow with a hand that is no longer cold. The ink dries faster there than anywhere else.
Meridine receives the vows at low water. Numen weighs each page down with a different stone, as though identical weights might imply identical words.
I am publishing what I erased.
All of it?
That is the portion causing difficulty.
The custodians have orders to preserve public calm. They have interpreted public with unusual precision and calm with none at all.
I wrote the order. It has outlived its excuse.
Can you rescind it?
It requires a truthful record. We are currently fighting over the paper.
Do not destroy their tablets. Those contain the names of the people I omitted.
Then we bring the tablets out with them.
The doors open onto a queue. Most people have come to find a relative, not an explanation of the world.
I prepared a speech.
Start with the index.
One undated record describes Kaelis carrying a warmth she did not kindle. Numen recognizes his handwriting and cannot tell whether it is memory or warning.
The archive has never reliably distinguished those things.
Will you tell her?
After I have stopped wanting the answer to be convenient.
It knows which page I am tempted to lose.
Hold that page where everyone can see it.
The remnant burns around the blank margin. The difficult sentence remains. Numen makes five copies before reading it again.
My vow is to keep the whole record, including the hand that altered it.
Put your name first.
The third vow returns with the published confession. Beneath each erased name is a space for corrections from the living.
Truth is not a thing I can finish on their behalf.
Will the seal accept an unfinished record?
If it cannot, we are building another lie.
The root bridge has a gap at its center. Verdance says it marks the frontier. The people stranded above the ravine call it the missing part.
If we close it, soldiers can cross.
So can the people waiting behind them.
I was hoping for an easier answer.
The keepers permit departures but forbid returns. They say a vow to shelter strangers must end somewhere.
These people were strangers yesterday. Today they have houses here.
And seedlings. Some of them planted seedlings.
Then perhaps the roots already know them.
Leave the bridge standing.
It is the reason we are here.
The bridge grows a narrow crossing. Its handrails remain separate, with a rope between them for people who need help.
It did not heal shut.
A gap can be a choice instead of a wound.
Pyre deserters have built a toll furnace on the opposite bank. They burn the refugees' belongings and call it an entry fee.
I taught them that nothing should cross a border without paying.
Then tell them what you have learned since.
They are holding the road. They may require a demonstration.
Your pay is late. Their lives are not compensation.
We can settle the first problem after this.
The furnace is dismantled into cooking stoves. The soldiers' names go into the same relief ledger as everyone else's.
No oath of gratitude. Just sign that you received your share.
That is a much smaller piece of paper.
A message from Thornmaw asks whether the orchard still agrees. The keepers are offended. The refugees are relieved.
He said to ask each morning.
Even after we said yes?
Especially then.
The visitor comes to the kitchen after the last bowl is washed. There is no escort, no banner, and no request to see the queen.
A city that cooks together has understood more than its generals.
And a stranger who arrives after supper has understood less than its children.
We can wait.
The visitor leaves a coal that burns without fuel. Beside it is a note asking nothing in return. The hospital sends for it before the council can meet.
Does it open the seal?
It opens a hand. You may close it again.
Let us test the second part before we accept the first.
We did not ask it to cling.
Then help us make it let go.
The coal cools. The visitor kneels beside the injured stoker and waits while a mortal doctor works.
We are sorry. Kindness without a way to refuse is another appetite.
You sound as though you have practiced saying that.
Draxus orders every recipient detained. The hospital wards fill with guards, and nobody can reach the water pump.
The gift was dangerous. That does not make the sick criminals.
It makes them a breach.
They have names. Start there.
We are removing spears from a hospital. Remember how that should sound.
The patients stay where they can be treated.
The guards return to the gates. The patients keep their blankets. The Cantor departs without demanding a hearing.
A refusal is an answer. We will remember yours.
And I will remember that you waited for the doctor.
Kaelis opens her other hand. A second pale warmth moves beneath the iron. She has carried it since the cold kiln.
You should have told the council.
I wanted to know whether it was hope before you named it treason.
She does not surrender it. You do not pretend you failed to notice.
The restored names do not fit on the memorial wall. Numen asks the masons for more stone. They ask which names may be written smaller.
None.
We will need another wall.
Yes. I am learning to give expensive answers.
A woman has crossed two seas to remove her husband's name. He is alive in the southern islands. The archive demands proof that she is herself.
I once made certainty into an entrance requirement.
She has brought letters.
I will read them as though someone other than me can know a thing.
Protect the letters from the water.
And their owner from the archive.
The name is removed without erasing the place it occupied. Under it the mason writes that the record was corrected by someone who came back.
A memorial should be pleased to lose a name.
Put that above the door.
The Concord offers a shortened confession. It retains Numen's remorse and removes the people who benefited from his silence.
It is written beautifully.
That has been a persistent problem with our lies.
Will they publish the whole thing?
There is room in the light for an unflattering page.
Several, in this instance.
The unabridged record travels on public boats. The first correction arrives before the last copy has left the quay.
My vow has survived being contradicted.
It may be the first thing you have written that wanted to.
In the oldest binding Numen finds five marks around an empty place. Someone wrote: leave room for the one who says no.
Who wrote it?
The First Caller. Before she learned to call a lie protection.
He sends the page down the well-kept stair. This time he keeps no private copy from the others.
Seraphel opens the Mercy Gate. Petitioners arrive carrying the chains once used to turn them away. They want to know where to put them.
Here, where we will have to step around them.
Some will say that obstructs the entrance.
They obstructed it more effectively before.
The Inquisitor brings an oath binding every citizen to Seraphel's mercy. It has no provision for anyone who does not want it.
You are mercy.
Then listen when I tell you it cannot be compulsory.
Who is permitted to cross?
They may keep their faith. They may not use it as a lock.
The gate remains open after we win.
The oath is taken down. Several petitioners leave. Seraphel watches until they are safely beyond the walls.
That was harder than opening the gate.
It was the part that made opening it mean something.
Under the arch Seraphel's halo casts a second shadow. It knows a voice from before there were separate voices.
We never meant to make mercy lonely.
You made me able to leave. Do not call that a mistake.
Can you hold the gate while we clear the echo?
We could make their pain quiet.
First ask whether they want your quiet.
The second shadow withdraws. Outside the gate a petitioner curses Seraphel's name and continues home unharmed.
My vow is to protect the right to refuse me.
Including when you are right.
Seraphel signs without her halo's seal. The signature is awkward. She has always allowed the light to do that part for her.
Does it look like a person's name?
It looks like someone wrote it herself.
She asks for another page to practice on. The first is kept, with the uneven letters plainly visible.
Ravenna sits where her sister sat. Thornmaw has brought a cushion and been instructed to stop hovering. He has obeyed one instruction.
You have brought a committee into my cellar.
You asked for reports.
I hoped they would learn brevity on the stairs.
The stone tightens when the fifth vow is read. It has become accustomed to a single name that never changes its mind.
A lock remembers what worked, even when what worked was cruelty.
Then we shall be patient while it learns manners.
The stair stays open. That was the first condition.
Do not promise to take my place. Promise to ask whether I still choose it.
I will ask while the answer can still be no.
The pressure eases. Ravenna lifts one hand from her knee and reaches for the tea her sister has carried down.
Still dreadful.
You are welcome.
Numen's measurement would divide the burden into equal turns. It has no space for age, exhaustion, or someone who simply cannot continue.
It is an elegant schedule.
Then I advise you to mistrust it.
I will not be made the unit in which you measure endurance.
I forgot that an equal number can conceal an unequal cost.
Help us dismantle your conclusion.
Numen crosses out the schedule in front of everyone. He leaves the calculation readable beneath the correction.
My vow is to name the cost before asking anyone to carry it.
Include the one who asks.
Ravenna signs. The First Caller asks whether her own name is required. Nobody answers for her.
I shall need time.
We have spent a thousand years pretending we did not.
Above them five separate lights appear on the roofless table. For one evening nothing asks to be worshipped.
The five vows ring once across the city. Everyone hears the bell in a different street. For a moment the council mistakes agreement for success.
The intervals are narrowing.
Is that bad?
They are becoming the same interval. That is not what we wrote.
The Concord begins ringing the bell for the citizens. Attendance is consent; absence is a clerical delay.
You have made renewal into a head count.
People are busy. We are assisting them.
Then assist them by letting them answer.
Take down the attendance boards.
Nobody's silence will be used as a signature.
The bell loses half its strength. The five lights remain, uneven and distinct. Numen exhales as though the weakness is good news.
It is finally measuring something real.
Then we can finally repair what it shows us.
The rootkeepers withdraw for a day to harvest before the storm. Their absence strains the other lights. The council asks them to reconsider.
You said we could refuse.
We did.
Then why have you brought soldiers to ask us twice?
Their no is not an attack on the seal.
Our answer to it might be.
The militia withdraws. Four cities send harvesters instead of negotiators. At dusk the orchard renews without being asked a third time.
That was a better argument.
It was not supposed to be an argument.
When the bell rings again Kaelis answers before it sounds. Numen sees her mouth move a fraction ahead of everyone else's.
How did you know the moment?
I have been waiting for it all day.
It is a truthful answer. Numen writes it down and leaves room beneath it.
Kaelis leads you below the coal store. In five jars she has saved the ashes of the old forge. A pale heat passes between them without consuming anything.
It began before the Cantor came. I thought that mattered.
It matters. It does not make it safe.
I know. That is why you are here now.
Draxus follows with soldiers. He sees the warmth and reaches the obvious conclusion before Kaelis has finished speaking.
You ordered us to let the forge die. Then you kept its fire for yourself.
Yes. That is the part I have no defense for.
An admission is not permission to execute her.
Take my command. Leave the people in this room alive.
There will be a hearing with more than one possible ending.
Kaelis lays her command seal on the floor. Draxus picks it up without looking pleased. Neither has won what they wanted.
I can answer questions without a throne behind me.
Then start with the first warmth.
She repeats her vow. The second light answers honestly: strength spent to warm someone else. A thousand joined voices also meet that condition.
We did not change her words. We believed them.
You let me think the warmth was mine.
You let yourself think the difference would not matter.
It has been answering when I thought I was choosing.
Then choose now, while we can hear you.
The warmth leaves her gauntlet. Her hand is cold again. Across the city the second vow goes dark.
I promised warmth. I never promised to remain myself to give it.
That is what we must add, if you choose to sign again.
The vows have four signatures and one unmarked space. Kaelis asks Numen not to erase the first version.
Let them see how a true sentence became a lie.
And the part where you brought us here yourself.
Outside someone has begun singing the kitchen song in a voice that is not quite singular.
The cistern reflects five people as one figure. When Kaelis steps away the reflection does not change.
It is showing us a conclusion it reached before we arrived.
Can we make it show the evidence?
We can make it stop being our only witness.
The transcript has every speaker agreeing. The words are exact. The pauses between them have been removed.
That is where Ravenna changed her mind.
I recorded the silence as nothing.
Then the record lost the most important answer.
Keep the pauses. Even the ones that make us look uncertain.
Especially those.
The complete recording sounds slower, less certain, alive. The reflection gains a seam through its center.
There. We did not agree about what the warmth meant.
And she did not consent to what it became.
The Cantor arrives with people whose pain has eased. No chain binds them. They ask why you would take the quiet away.
You cannot rescue someone by refusing to hear their answer.
We are asking whether they can give a different one tomorrow.
Then ask them. We will wait outside.
One of them asked to step outside. The water would not let her.
Then we start by making room for that answer.
One witness leaves. Four choose to stay. The Cantor does not call the departing woman back.
Our mercy is unfinished too.
Keep that in your next song.
Numen adds a clause to every vow: I remain someone who may choose otherwise. The ink divides the reflection into five.
Will a sentence do it?
No. A sentence tells us what we must do. I have mistaken those things before.
The corrected pages leave on five boats. Each carries the full record of why the correction was needed.
The nursery's roots have joined every tree to one ring. Their fruit ripens without water. The gardeners fear how well it works.
We have never fed so many people.
What happens if one tree wants different soil?
We tried moving one. The others screamed.
The keepers demand time to study the abundance. In the seed house roots close around the traveling pots.
A forest is not one tree repeated until the horizon gives up.
Can you reach them from below the city?
I can ask. The answer must be theirs.
The small pots first. They still have separate roots.
Then we keep it that way.
The gardeners carry seedlings through a passage the oldest tree opened beneath the wall. It has refused the ring from inside it.
I should have trusted it to choose.
You can begin now.
Cutting the pale root-ring will lose this season's harvest. Keeping it will lose the next season's seeds.
We will need food from four cities.
Ashmar will send what it has.
It has so little.
Then we will be hungry separately, and help each other. Those are allowed together.
The gardeners are clear. Cut the binding.
The fruit falls before it ripens. Beneath it five kinds of seed remain. The gardeners collect them in separate baskets.
I wanted there to be no cost.
So did everyone who built the old locks.
The first relief cart contains turnips. A note from Draxus says the army can manage on beans.
He is making an apology badly.
It still feeds people.
For the first time since the forge went cold Kaelis laughs without any other voice arriving with hers.
A water-mirror carries Ravenna from the stair. The council reconvenes with Kaelis's iron chair empty. She stands beside it until Seraphel asks whether she intends to remain there all day.
I do not know whether I am still welcome to sit.
Then ask us. Do not turn our answer into something you punish yourself with.
Sit while we decide what comes next.
The Inquisitor presents a cleaner binding with four vows. It names Ashmar a containment district and calls the omission necessary symmetry.
Four is symmetrical. It is also the wrong number of cities.
One of them betrayed the others.
A city is not a woman, and a woman is not her worst answer.
Remove the district order. Leave the witnesses their seats.
We are not improving the old lie by making it smaller.
The fourfold diagram is kept beside the original as a warning. Kaelis returns to the iron chair without her command seal.
Now we can hear you without the chair speaking first.
I should have tried this years ago.
Below the table the withdrawn warmth gathers every accusation into a shape. It offers Kaelis a role everyone understands.
They would find it easier to forgive a monster than a neighbor who made a choice.
Yes. I would find it easier too.
Then let it remain difficult.
I am responsible. I am not all that happened.
We will keep both truths in the room.
The shape thins. Nobody applauds. Draxus places a relief ledger beside Kaelis and asks her to check the sums.
You are trusting me with fuel?
I am asking you to count it where I can see.
The corrected fifth place waits. Kaelis adds a clause: I will not make another person's silence into permission to save them.
That leaves you with fewer grand gestures.
I have a ledger to finish.
The second light returns, smaller than before. It keeps its own time.
The Cantor's procession enters Ashmar with blankets, fuel, and no weapons the guards can recognize. Half the city welcomes it.
We have brought enough for everyone.
Then leave enough for the people who will not join you.
Show us where they live.
Draxus closes the inner streets. Families split between the procession and kiln begin calling each other prisoners.
I cannot tell who is still themselves.
Then ask a smaller question. Who is trying to go home?
Start by opening their street.
Nobody is required to stand on our side to pass.
Keep the route clear in both directions.
People cross toward both fires. Some carry blankets from the procession to neighbors who refused it. Nobody stops them.
I have no formation for this.
Then stand where someone can ask for help.
At the great forge a white flame climbs without fuel. The Cantor turns to it with the same alarm you feel.
We offered warmth. We did not offer the city.
We could hold all of you. None would need to stand outside again.
And the people who want the door?
I know that warmth. I know how much it leaves unsaid.
Then we will help you keep it from taking them.
The white flame breaks into sparks. The Cantor carries a burned child to the doctor who treated the stoker.
You were right about the door.
You were right about the blankets.
The procession departs smaller. Some remain because they have found work. Others leave because they found the quiet they wanted.
We have not ended this.
No. We have kept a city able to argue tomorrow.
Above the cold forge hundreds of separate fires answer the night.
Numen builds five beacons with different intervals. The seal must carry an answer without smoothing away the person who sent it.
Agreement should travel. Identity should not have to travel with it.
Can you do that?
I can test whether I have failed before we put cities inside it.
The tide-engine waits for identical answers before proceeding. It was designed by someone who feared errors more than silence.
That someone was me.
I have noticed a pattern in your introductions.
I am trying to end it without falsifying it.
We keep all five intervals, even if the machine calls them noise.
Especially if it calls them noise.
The engine accepts a staggered sequence. Five lamps remain five lamps. The water between them is dark and ordinary.
A successful absence.
Put that in the engineering report.
The Concord's relay replaces Seraphel's answer with a permanent yes. Its engineers call it a precaution against her being absent.
If I am absent, send someone to ask why.
The seal cannot wait on a person.
Then it is already the wrong seal.
Let it go dark until I answer.
The others know how to wait now.
One lamp goes out. Four carry the strain without joining. When Seraphel answers her light returns in its imperfect rhythm.
It can survive a pause.
Now teach it to survive an honest no.
It cannot. At a full refusal the signals meet in the empty center and become one. Numen marks the failure in red.
What keeps the center empty?
Someone must carry the distance while the others renew. Outside the warmth, able to leave it.
Kaelis reads the measurement twice. This time she asks everyone else to read it with her.
Seraphel prepares to step into the empty center. Her halo fits the measurement perfectly. That is what frightens her.
I was made for this shape.
That does not decide whether you must take it.
I know. I am waiting to discover whether I believe myself.
The Concord kneels and thanks her for a sacrifice she has not offered. Their gratitude fills the garden like a locked gate.
The people need you.
They needed me yesterday. I was allowed to be a person then.
Stand up. Let her answer without your knees on the scale.
I am not refusing mercy. I am refusing your ownership of it.
Clear a path back out of the circle.
The guard stands. Seraphel steps away and discovers that the world has not ended because she wanted to remain in it.
No.
We heard you.
Through the water-mirror Ravenna watches Thornmaw send a root into the circle. He meant to spare them the question. It is the same mistake in an older shape.
I know how to wait.
You also know how to mistake waiting for a life.
Will you withdraw it if we ask?
Yes. I can withdraw it.
Then do. We are practicing a different answer.
The root lifts. Grass survived beneath it. Thornmaw says nothing for a long time, and nobody fills the silence for him.
I would like to see the orchard again.
We will make that possible too.
Kaelis asks for the outer watch. The costs are read before she offers: distance, the loss of shared warmth, and no promise of return.
I am not paying for a pardon. If you make it that, refuse me.
We may still ask you to stay.
I know. That is what makes this a choice.
The vows descend the well-kept stair. Ravenna remains at the stone. Her sister carries the fifth light; Thornmaw walks beside her instead of in front.
There is still time to choose differently.
Read the cost again.
All of it.
The chamber remembers the Unanswered. Old weather gathers around every promise, waiting to discover which will become another prison.
It is what I left behind. Do not call it fate to spare my feelings.
We will not.
And we will not put someone back in my place to make the story tidy.
The old stone stays held until the new seal answers. We do not gamble with the people above.
We make room without letting go too early.
The weather breaks against five separate lights. The stair remains visible through it, every lamp still burning.
A way back. We remembered.
Keep remembering after I have gone.
Beyond the lattice the Voice offers Kaelis the sound of her city before the forge died. Every hammer is exactly where she remembers it.
We could return what you lost. We could make the cold mean something.
It already means people needed fuel. I do not need a god to make their hunger important.
We did not want you to suffer alone.
Then let me stand apart without calling it abandonment.
We will answer from here.
Kaelis opens her hand. The warmth leaves. She steps onto the outer causeway with an ordinary coal, knowing it will eventually go out.
We do not understand.
Neither did I. Keep listening.
The lattice closes around an empty center. Kaelis is beyond its warmth, her red light distinct. The binding holds. Ravenna rises from the stone.
Are you coming upstairs?
Slowly. I have spent a great deal of time planning a dignified answer.
Thornmaw takes the flask. Nobody crowns the person who stood apart. They write down how to ask whether she still chooses it.
On the first morning everyone wakes before the beacons. Quiet has been mistaken for safety often enough that nobody celebrates yet.
The outer watch has answered.
What did she say?
That the coal is nearly out. And yes, today.
The orchard withholds renewal while a relief cart is trapped behind a militia toll. The seal dims. Nobody proposes forcing the orchard to answer.
We promised to feed people. They are stopping the food.
Then we know which part needs fixing.
A vow should lead us toward the work, not replace it.
Let the cart through. Nobody has to swear anything to eat.
I will tell the orchard we remembered.
The cart crosses. A green beacon answers after breakfast. Across the valleys four other lights keep their different intervals.
I am at the orchard. It has grown badly in several places.
Will you stay?
The Cantor left a letter naming a village that chose the Communion. Every signature differs. All the signatures end at the same moment.
We have learned to leave the door open. We ask you to visit those who choose to stay.
There is an echo in the paper.
Then we clear the echo before we decide what the people mean.
A choice made freely still deserves a witness.
And a witness must be able to hear an unwelcome answer.
The echo fades. The signatures remain. The village is real, and no army stands outside waiting to be defeated.
I cannot mark this resolved.
Leave the page open.
Ravenna takes tea in the garden. Her sister leaves before sunset to see another city. Thornmaw sends an account of the orchard, including every mistake.
I can hear morning birds from here. Tell me which ones they are.
I will ask. Will you answer tomorrow?
Ask me tomorrow.
Five cups stand on the table. One cools beside an empty chair. Beyond the valleys a village sings in a single gentle voice. You pack the invitation, and go to listen.
